# The Starter

Somewhere in a kitchen in San Francisco, or Alaska, or a village in the Auvergne, there is a jar of flour paste that someone will tell you is a hundred years old. They will say it came over on a wagon, or survived a war tucked in a coat pocket, or was kept alive by a great-grandmother who fed it every morning before she fed herself. They will hand you a spoonful in a yogurt container with masking tape on the lid, and you will carry it home carefully, as if it were an egg, or a relic.

It is a lovely story, and in the most literal sense it is almost certainly false.

A sourdough starter is a community of wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria living in a slurry of flour and water. Every time you feed it, you discard most of the old culture and add fresh flour, which carries its own microbes. The environment of your kitchen, the air, your hands, and the particular grain all push on that community. Microbiologists who have studied starters find that within weeks, a culture carried from one place to another tends to drift toward something shaped by its new home. The organisms in your great-grandmother's jar are long gone, replaced many thousands of generations over by their descendants and by newcomers who wandered in and stayed.

So what, exactly, is a hundred years old?

This is the Ship of Theseus in a mason jar. The Greeks told of a ship preserved in Athens whose rotting planks were replaced one by one until none of the original wood remained, and they argued about whether it was still the same ship. Philosophers have been worrying at the puzzle for two and a half thousand years, adding complications: what if someone gathered the discarded planks and rebuilt the original? Which one is the real ship then?

I've come to think that the sourdough starter offers a more forgiving answer than the ship does, because nobody ever really cared about the planks. What made the ship the ship, for the Athenians, was that it was *kept*. It was maintained by a city that remembered what it stood for. Its identity lived in the act of tending, not in the timber.

The starter makes this obvious in a way the ship doesn't. There is no pretense that the substance persists. Every baker knows they throw most of it away each day. What persists is the *practice*: the morning feeding, the particular ratio of flour to water, the habit of checking whether it has doubled, the smell you learn to recognize as "ready" and the sharper, nail-polish smell that means you've neglected it. What gets handed down in that yogurt container isn't really a population of microorganisms. It's an invitation into a rhythm.

And the rhythm is old. That part is true. Humans have been leavening bread with wild cultures for thousands of years, long before anyone knew what yeast was. For most of that history, the knowledge was carried entirely by practice. You didn't understand fermentation; you just knew that if you saved a lump of yesterday's dough and worked it into today's, the bread would rise. Bakers passed along a technique that worked for reasons nobody could explain, and the technique outlived every individual who performed it.

There's something humbling in that. We tend to imagine that continuity requires permanence, that for a thing to last, some core of it must remain unchanged. But many of the most durable things in human life don't work that way at all. Languages last for millennia while every word in them shifts in sound and meaning. A university can be eight hundred years old without a single brick or professor from its founding. A family can feel continuous across generations while sharing, after a few removes, only a sliver of genetic material with any particular ancestor. Your own body replaces most of its cells over the years, and you still answer to your name.

What these things have in common is not substance but pattern, and pattern sustained by care. A language survives because people keep speaking it to their children. A university survives because people keep deciding it's worth running. A starter survives because someone keeps feeding it. The moment the tending stops, the continuity ends, and no amount of original material can bring it back. You could freeze-dry the great-grandmother's culture and preserve every original microbe, and it would be, in a sense, *less* alive as a tradition than the constantly replaced jar on the counter.

I find this a comforting way to think about inheritance. It means that the things we receive from the past aren't museum pieces we're obligated to keep pristine. They're more like fires we're asked to keep burning, and fire is never the same flame twice. The starter that arrives in your kitchen will become yours. It will take on the character of your flour and your drafty windows and your tendency to forget it on weekends. The bread will taste a little different from the bread your friend makes with the "same" starter. This isn't a corruption of the lineage. It is the lineage. Adaptation is how living things stay alive.

There's a responsibility in this too. If continuity lives in practice rather than in matter, then it's fragile in a particular way. It can't be stored. It can only be done. Every tradition that matters to anyone is, at any given moment, only as alive as the people currently bothering to perform it. That's a little frightening. It's also a kind of power. You don't need to own anything original to be a legitimate inheritor. You only need to show up and do the thing.

So when someone hands you a jar and tells you it's a hundred years old, the honest reply isn't to correct them about microbial succession. The honest reply is to say thank you, take it home, and feed it tomorrow morning. The story is false about the flour and true about everything else. The jar is a hundred years old in the only way that ever really mattered: somebody, every single day for a century, decided to keep it going.

Now it's your turn.
